title: Barista Express or Pro still too fast at grind setting 1? Check these in order before buying a grinder
description: Barista Express or Pro still fast at setting 1? Check beans, basket, dose and burrs in order, then move the upper burr finer, before you buy a grinder.
primaryQuery: breville barista express grinder won't grind fine enough
relatedQueries: barista express shots too fast on setting 1
breville upper burr adjustment which way
barista express sour espresso finest grind
should I buy a separate grinder for barista express
body:
Don't buy a grinder yet. If your Barista Express or Barista Pro still pours fast, sour and thin at grind setting 1, there are a handful of checks that cost nothing, and Breville's own booklet backs every one of them: fresh beans, the right basket, a full dose, clean burrs, and then moving the upper burr finer, one number at a time. Most people who ask this question haven't done all of them. Go through them in order and stop at the first one that slows the shot. A new grinder is the last step, not the first.

First, what setting 1 actually means. On the Express the dial runs from 1 (finest) to 16 (coarsest), and Breville suggests starting at 5. On the Pro it runs from 1 to 30, with 15 as the default. If you're on 1, you've run out of dial. That doesn't mean you've run out of grinder. There's more adjustment inside, and you'll get to it below. But the outside dial can't help you any more, so the next fix has to come from somewhere else.

## The test you can run tonight

You don't need tools or to take anything apart. Make one shot and check four things.

**The bag.** Look for a "Roasted On" date. A "Best Before" date doesn't count. Breville recommends using beans 5–20 days after roasting, and the Pro booklet says outright that stale coffee "may pour too quickly from the portafilter and taste bitter and watery." That describes your problem exactly. Supermarket beans without a roast date are the most common culprit, so if that's what you're using, buy a fresh bag before you go any further.

**The basket.** Breville includes two kinds. Single-wall baskets are for fresh whole beans. Dual-wall (pressurised) baskets are for pre-ground coffee, and in Breville's words they "regulate the pressure and help to optimize the extraction regardless of the grind, dose and tamp pressure or freshness." With a dual-wall basket in, the basket is doing the work, so changing the grind tells you very little. Diagnose with a single-wall basket.

**The dose.** Tamp firmly (Breville says 22–33 lb), then check where the tamper's metal cap sits. It should be level with the basket rim. If it sinks below the rim, you're under-dosing. A double basket is designed for about 16–19 g. On the Pro, Breville adds that a finer grind in a single-wall basket may need more coffee.

**The timing.** Start a timer when you press the button and note when the espresso starts to flow. Breville's Pro guide says 8–12 seconds is normal and under 7 seconds means too little coffee or too coarse a grind. The Express guide describes an under-extracted shot as starting after 1–6 seconds and finishing within 20, against a target of 25–30 seconds.

This order comes from Breville. Both troubleshooting tables give the same three causes for "Espresso runs out too quickly": grind too coarse, not enough coffee, tamped too lightly. Neither lists the burrs. That's why the burrs come last here.

The troubleshooter on this page walks through the same questions one at a time and stops at the first one that fixes the shot.

## Clean the burrs before you move them

If fresh beans, a single-wall basket and a full dose still give you a shot that gushes, clean the grinder. Breville's procedure: empty the hopper, run the grinder empty, take out the top burr, and brush both burrs and the chute. Breville says this "removes oil build-up on the burrs which can impede performance." It's free, it takes a few minutes, and you have to take the top burr out anyway for the next step. Skip the advanced clean that removes the lower burr. Breville says it's only needed for a blockage. Both booklets also warn that the burrs are extremely sharp, so handle them by the edges.

## Move the upper burr toward fine, one number at a time

Forum threads are full of "never touch the internal burr" and "shim it." Breville's US booklets say something different. They call the adjustable upper burr "a feature of your Barista Express" (and of the Barista Pro) that extends the grind range, because "some types of coffee may require a wider grind range."

The procedure, condensed from the booklet:

1. Unlock the hopper, empty the beans into a container, refit the hopper and run the grinder until it's empty.
2. Remove the hopper, then lift out the upper burr by its wire handle. On the Express the booklet shows no tools for this, and the Allen key in the box is for the shower-screen seal.
3. Unclip the wire handle, write down the number the burr is on now, and turn the adjustable ring **one number toward finer**.
4. Line the number up with the handle opening, refit the handle, push the burr in firmly, lock it, and refit and lock the hopper.
5. Pull a shot with the same beans and the same dose, and time it again.

Breville recommends one adjustment at a time, and so do I. If one step slows the shot a little but not enough, repeat.

About direction: finer is the side you want when shots run fast. At least one well-known retailer guide tells readers with fast shots at the finest setting to go coarser. That's the wrong way for your problem. The Pro booklet's illustrations show the ring marked FINE and COARSE, so follow the ring, not the forum.

**What the booklet doesn't say.** Neither US booklet gives the range of numbers on the ring, the factory position, any warning about the burrs touching, or whether adjusting the burr affects the warranty. You'll see a factory number repeated online, but it comes from blogs, not Breville, so don't rely on it. That's why you write down your starting number. My rule, which is a judgement and not a Breville instruction: if the grinder starts to sound like metal on metal, or one more step finer makes no difference to the shot, go back one number and stop there.

If you're turning the burr finer to grind very light roasts, note that Breville warns against grinding green or under-roasted beans. It says they're too dense and not brittle enough for a burr grinder and can damage or break the burrs.

Here's one owner's experience. It's a single report, not a spec, but it fits the pattern. On the Singletrack forum this autumn, someone with a refurbished Barista Pro was getting gritty, chunky grounds and only a passable shot through the pressurised basket. They cleaned the grinder, moved the internal burr from 2 to 1 with the dial at 2, and reported a 28-second shot that was "WAY better." Breville also offered them a free upper burr, but the improvement came before that burr arrived.

## Still fast? Check your date code and call Breville

You've done everything above: fresh beans, single-wall basket, cap level with the rim, clean burrs, the upper burr as fine as it goes without contact. If shots still run fast, the burr itself is the next suspect. Before buying anything, look at the model sticker under the machine and find the production date code (PDC). An Australian parts seller lists two different upper burrs for these machines: SP0001801 for machines built before PDC 1926, and SP0027464 for machines from 1926 (2019, week 26) onwards. That comes from a parts listing, not a Breville spec, and US pricing and availability weren't checked.

Contact Breville support before you order. The booklet's warranty covers repair or replacement when the machine is "defective due to faulty materials, workmanship, or function," and a machine that can't grind fine enough with fresh beans could reasonably count. At least one owner was sent a free burr. Have your date code and shot times ready when you call.

## Keep the machine

For most people this ends with fresh beans, the right basket, a clean grinder and the upper burr a step or two finer, and the machine you already own pulls a proper 25–30 second shot. That's the outcome I'd expect, and it's the one to aim for.

## When I'd choose differently

**You've done every step and it's still fast.** Fresh beans, single-wall basket, full dose, clean burrs, upper burr as fine as it goes without contact, and Breville either can't help or the replacement burr didn't change anything. At that point the built-in grinder has reached its limit, and a separate espresso grinder is the honest answer. Keep the built-in one as a backup.

**You mainly drink very light roasts.** This is my own judgement, not something Breville says. If very light roasts are what you want, you'll be working at the fine end of the built-in grinder every day, and Breville warns that under-roasted beans can damage its burrs. A separate grinder makes more sense for you than for someone happy with medium roasts.

**You just bought a refurbished unit and the grounds look gritty or chunky.** Run the checks, but call the seller or Breville early. The owner in the forum report got a free burr offer, and a fault on a newly bought machine is the seller's problem, not yours.

## How this guide was put together

We read the current US instruction booklets for the Barista Express (BES870, X26 edition) and Barista Pro (BES878, Q26 edition) page by page: grind settings, filter baskets, extraction guide, burr cleaning, "Adjusting Conical Burrs", troubleshooting and the warranty paragraph. We also read Breville's US grind-size tutorial for the Pro, two Australian parts-seller listings for the upper burr, Seattle Coffee Gear's top-burr guide, a blog post on the inner burr, and an owner thread on the Singletrack forum. We compared what these sources say against each other and against the booklets.

What we did not do: we did not test either machine or any burr setting. We did not confirm the upper-burr number range, the factory position or burr-contact behaviour, because neither booklet states them. We did not ask Breville support about the warranty, or check US prices and availability for replacement burrs. We did not research standalone grinders for this question, so we don't recommend one here. The owner report is one person's experience.

Sources:

- Breville Barista Express BES870 US instruction booklet (X26): https://assets.breville.com/BES870/BES870_USCM_IB_X26_LR.pdf
- Breville Barista Pro BES878 US instruction booklet (Q26): https://assets.breville.com/BES878/BES878_USCM_IB_Q26_LR.pdf
- Breville US, Barista Pro: how to adjust grind size: https://breville.com/inspiration/en-us/tutorials/the-barista-pro/first-time-setup/how-to-adjust-grind-size
- Singletrack forum owner thread, Sage/Breville Barista Pro grinder (Aug–Sep 2026): https://singletrackworld.com/forum/off-topic/sage-breville-barista-pro-grinder/
- Ricambi listing, upper burr SP0027464 (from 1926 PDC): https://www.ricambi.com.au/breville-barista-express-upper-burr-from-pdc-1926
- Ricambi listing, upper burr kit SP0001801 (pre-1926 PDC): https://www.ricambi.com.au/breville-coffee-machine-outer-upper-burr-grinder-k
